podcast.title: The Rural Purge (1970-1971)
podcast.body: Under the leadership of Fred Silverman, who took over CBS in 1970-1971, the network underwent a significant programming shift known as the "rural purge." This initiative systematically canceled any show perceived as "remotely country," regardless of its ratings, including popular programs like The Johnny Cash Show, Petticoat Junction, The Beverly Hillbillies, The Red Skelton Show, Green Acres, and even The Ed Sullivan Show. The move was replaced by "urban friendly programming" such as All in the Family, MASH, and The Mary Tyler Moore Show, driven by a desire to target more heavily populated areas for higher ratings. "he gutted the network of any show that seemed remotely country. It did not matter what the ratings were."

podcast.title: Controversial Contract with The Clash (January 25, 1977)
podcast.body: CBS Records signed The Clash to a worldwide contract for 129,000 pounds on January 25, 1977. This deal was highly controversial among punk's hardcore fans, who viewed it as a betrayal of punk's anti-establishment ethos and declared it "the day Punk died," despite The Clash's stated intention to "subvert the record industry from within."

podcast.body: CBS signed The Clash to a record deal on January 25, 1977, after their emergence on the British punk scene. "As far as British punk went, the clash finally signed a record deal with CBS on the 25th."

podcast.title: The Clash Signing Controversy (1977)
podcast.body: CBS Records signed The Clash to a worldwide recording contract for 100,000 pounds on January 25, 1977, amidst a fierce bidding war. This deal was widely condemned by the punk community as a betrayal of the genre's anti-establishment ethos, with one fanzine even declaring "punk died the day the clash signed to CBS." "And on January 25, 1977, at the very height of punk rock in the UK, they signed a worldwide recording contract with CBS records for 100,000 pounds."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Concept of Selling Out: Part 1

podcast.title: The Clash's Controversial Signing (1977)
podcast.body: On January 26, 1977, CBS Records signed The Clash to a major label deal valued at 100,000 pounds, a figure significantly higher than other competing offers. This decision sparked widespread condemnation within the British punk community, who viewed it as a "sell out" for a band previously seen as ideologically pure and anti-establishment, leading to protests throughout the UK. "The date was January 26, 1977. That's when the clash signed a major record deal with CBS."

podcast.title: MTV Racism Challenge (1983)
podcast.body: CBS Records allegedly threatened to withdraw all their videos from MTV if the channel did not begin to feature Black artists. This action is credited with forcing MTV to cave and start showing videos from Michael Jackson's "Thriller" album, breaking the channel's unofficial color barrier. "It wasn't until CBS records allegedly threatened to pull all their videos from the channel that MTV caved and started to show videos from the thriller album."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rise and Fall and Future of the Music Video - Part 1

podcast.title: Pressure on MTV for Black Artist Airplay (1983)
podcast.body: CBS Records reportedly threatened to withhold all their music videos from MTV unless the channel played Michael Jackson's early 1983 hit "Billie Jean." This legendary move is credited with forcing MTV, which had largely refused to play videos by black artists, to begin regularly rotating clips by black musicians. "Legend has it that the channel largely refused to play videos by black artists before CBS records threatened to withhold all of their videos unless MTV played Jackson's early 1983 hit Billy Jean."

podcast.title: Worldwide CD Launch (March 1983)
podcast.body: CBS Records participated in the big worldwide launch of the compact disc format in March 1983, releasing 16 albums on the new format. This included major titles like Michael Jackson's "Thriller," helping to establish the CD in the market. "Then came the big worldwide launch in March of 1983, when CBS records released 16 albums on the new format, including Thriller from Michael Jackson."

podcast.title: CBS Columbia System
podcast.body: CBS Records developed and offered its own distinct stereo system, known as the Columbia system. This proprietary solution was one of several attempts by record companies to establish a viable method for stereo record production. "CBS records came up with their Columbia system."

podcast.body: CBS was noted by critic John Leonard for its unique capability to produce variety show "production numbers" with an "inspired comic touch," particularly when programming for audiences "over the mental age of eight." This quality was observed in shows like The Smothers Brothers Show, The Carol Burnett Show, and The Sonny & Cher Show. "Clive Davis, the president of CBS Records, offered Gamble and Huff a deal that allows them to create Philadelphia international records."

podcast.title: Refusal to Release The Clash's Debut in North America
podcast.body: CBS Records initially refused to release The Clash's self-titled debut album in North America for two years after its British release. Executives believed the record was "too raw, and abrasive, and crude, and political for American tastes" during the disco era. This decision forced North American fans to buy higher-priced British import versions, which astonishingly sold 100,000 copies, making it the biggest-selling import ever at the time, before CBS finally relented in 1979 with a "watered down version."

podcast.title: Rejection of "Bat Out of Hell"
podcast.body: Under the leadership of Clive Davis, CBS Records notably refused to sign or release Meat Loaf's debut album, *Bat Out of Hell*. Davis explicitly told songwriter Jim Steinman that he believed Steinman had "no idea how to write a rock song." "CBS Records, which was run by the legendary Clive Davis, said via Clive Davis that, no way, be making this. In fact, Clive Davis told Jim Steinman, clearly you have no idea how to write a rock song."

podcast.title: Reluctance Over Double and Triple Albums
podcast.body: CBS Records expressed reluctance to release The Clash's *London Calling* as a double album and *Sandinista!* as a triple album, due to concerns about manufacturing hassle and market price. The band had to make significant financial concessions, such as accepting lower royalty rates for *London Calling* and foregoing royalties on the first 200,000 copies of *Sandinista!*, to convince the label to release these ambitious projects.

podcast.title: Surpassed by Independent Labels
podcast.body: Major record labels like CBS, EMI, and Westpavogs were significantly outsold by the newly created independent labels Blanco y Negro Music and Max Music during the height of the Megamix phenomenon in Spain. This was a surprising development that disrupted the traditional market hierarchy. "superando a gigantes como CBS, Emmy, Westpavogs."

podcast.title: The Clash's Unfavorable Record Deal
podcast.body: The Clash's manager, Bernie Rhodes, negotiated a deal with CBS that committed the band to 13 albums at a significantly low royalty rate, a deal they believed was for only five albums. This unfavorable contract contributed to the band falling deeply into debt and was a major factor in Rhodes's initial firing. "The clash thought Bernie had negotiated a deal with CBS for five albums, one per year for five years. What actually happened is that Rose signed them up to a total of 13 albums at a really low royalty rate."
